text:
The definition of "real" performance is mostly irrelevant and here is why:

If what Nvidia claims is true (i.e., no downsides apart from overall latency, meaning smoother flow and better detail in movement), then your concerns, and those of many others, are completely invalid.

In the end, it doesn’t matter whether the frames are technically "true" or not. What really matters is what you see and feel. As I mentioned, apart from slightly higher latencies in particularly competitive FPS games, there are no downsides if Nvidia's claims hold up.

Additionally, the competitive games you’re concerned about are not very visually demanding, so you’ll still get more than enough FPS in those titles, generally speaking.

Nvidia knows exactly what they’re doing, and everyone else is just following suit. They understand that to drive screens now and in the near future, like 8K, silicon shrinks can’t keep up with the rapid development of screen tech (resolution). For context, 4K is around 8 million pixels, while 8K is about 33 million. There’s no way to approach that using node shrinks. Since we're nearing the end of the silicon era (i.e., no further shrinking is possible) and no real alternative exists yet, at least to my knowledge, the logical solution is to turn to AI, which Nvidia has done.

Even if Nvidia had scrapped the AI component and focused on a more traditional approach (more CUDA cores), the performance gains would likely have been limited to about 50%. Look at where we are now—moving from less than 30 FPS to over 200 FPS in the most demanding games. Without DLSS, and instead with a traditional performance boost of +50%, we’d be looking at something like 45 FPS in Cyberpunk at 4K resolution, compared to the sub-30 FPS we saw without it. Even the most casual observer can see why this traditional approach wouldn’t have worked.

text: What I don't like is that you are buying a product called a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) and now you are essentially paying for an accessory to the product, rather than a faster GPU. It's like buying a Ferrari in 2000 and it has a larger engine,  than a Ferrari in 2020, but the car in 2020 comes with traction control. The issue, is you aren't really getting a "faster" core product, but rather an accessory to the product that helps it perform better in slippery situations. The "Slippery" situations would be represented by the "Ray-Tracing" gimmick and support for "DLSS". So when the "weather" is bad, you really want to have your Traction Control so you can maintain your speed. It's almost as if they Sold the Weather to us, so that the Traction Control was required. I don't like this notion of not getting a product where the engine is markedly faster.  Additionally, only 25% of the frames you'll see are real. Think about that. You are paying for the "illusion of graphical information", like a house with a Ocean view, but the ocean view is a window which has a painted ocean on it.

text:
Framegen in general is a good thing if the native rendered FPS is already high enough (~>60 FPS at least).
If the card can render only 30 FPS an the 4x FG throws out 200 FPS, the game looks extremly fluid, but the responsiveness will be like 30 FPS.
Thats the reason why their marketing presentation line "5070 has 4090 performance" is nonsense. They compared the 5070 with full 4x FG and DLSS against the native rendering 4090. As soon as you activate 2x FG and DLSS on a 4090 it will still be higher Framerate and much more responsive as to higher native FPS.
author: @Napfkuchen

text: "but the responsiveness will be like 30 FPS": no it will be way worse. It will be around 15-20 fps or worse. First the you need to wait for the new frame to be generated (that is your normal 30 fps latency) then wait for the intermediate frame generated and displayed in place of the real one, wait again some milliseconds for correct pacing and then display the real frame. In my opinion you need at least 90-100 normal fps before thinking about to switch on FG. Depends on the game of course, but in my experience in CP77, 50 fps was too low to turn on FG, and I'm just a casual, single player only guy who grew up on playing games 25-30 fps.

Also latency will feel much worse with this than with standard frame gen - you get 2x the latency for the frame rate you see (60fps latency at 120 fps) with this 4x frame gen you get 4x the latency for what you see (60 fps latency at 240 fps) - that will objectively feel bad because what your eyes see isnt the response you feel. If your display is less than 144 hz, this tech is essentially useless unless you want the latency feel of 36 fps.

Maybe the 3x variant could be useful in some slow single player cases.

text:
Stupid response. The technology is fine, and it opens up the door for more mobile devices running higher fidelity graphics. Many of you seem to think there is some magic trick to dev game optimization, but its a really low IQ way to look at it. A lot of times that includes using techniques like mirroring geometry or overlapping UVs, using multiple low rez textures over a higher rez, baking lighting and shadow details into a scene and removing dynamic lighting...etc You don't understand that not only is that extremely time consuming and expensive, but it doesn't actually make the game look better. Many developers long to move away from those techniques of the past, and we can now do that with better software solutions WHICH does include frame gen. 

There is nothing wrong with frame gen and upscaling. Eventually we will get to a point where we don't even need to UV  game assets or worry about faking lighting detail. Most of what you see today, without the frame gen, is about faking visuals. If the latter is fine, so is frame gen.

author: @Koozwad

text:
@Koozwad  dismissing you after saying graphics have barely progressed after crysis.

That's some batshit insane talk
We have had massive leaps that people take for granted at this point hat you don't even think about it. Displacement mapping, tesselation, complex materials, subsurface scattering, global illumination, seamless enormous open worlds with practically limitless render distances, huge leaps in geometry complexity, in particle systems and particle counts. Real time ray traced reflections, lighting, shadows.

The list is insane, you just don't pay attention to the advancements because they happen on small individual feature scale across hundreds of games every year.

Also, of course rasterization is dead because we are reaching physical limitations for transistor sizes and amounts in a die without melting it. Inference isn't "fake" it's a different method of computation that is orders of magnitude more efficient than brute forcing it.

It's the same reason physics haven't been able to advance because simulating complex physics is insanely computation heavy in real time and inference is what will bring us shit like real time complex fluid dynamics and simulation because traditional logic computation can't, same with path tracing

From this material, anyone who has taken a maths class will calculate that the increase in native performance of the 5080 relative to the 4080Super is a maximum of 10 %. 
5080FGx2=560%
5080FGx4=960%
960/560=171%
5080FGx4/4080SuperFGx2 = 188%
188% compared to 171% is a 10% increase, which directly translates into native performance.

text:
​ @iris4547  You're confusing latency and throughput. A game running at 120FPS has a throughput of 8.33ms, but its latency is always much higher.
It'll be rendering some frame on the GPU, whilst it's doing all the gameplay, AI, and physics calculations for the next frame. That alone adds a 2x multiplier to latency, but without it, you'd be halving your frame rate, which would have a similar 2x multiplier impact to latency, so that's why it's worth doing (if the CPU workload is significant).

If you look at real-world testing on FG, you can see it doesn't add much overhead beyond holding the one frame, usually about 17-18ms for a game running at 60FPS. At 30FPS, FG makes no sense.

In my experience, FG just feels bad on KB+M, but I suspect it's got just as much to do with the blurrier nature due to the more extreme and unpredictable movements made by mouse rather than controller, than just the additional input latency, as well as the inconsistent frame delivery in many titles using it. For games like Cyberpunk, on a controller, it was a significant improvement for me. I'm skeptical that 3X or 4X modes will actually be a boon, seems like it'd just invite a lot more artifacts, for marginal returns, as 60->120 is much more impactful than 120->180 or 120->240 imo.

text:
The biggest problem isn't that frame generation adds latency. The problem is that it masks bad performance and existing latency.
Directly comparing the latency of frame generation misses the big picture. Negligible latency with frame generation turned on assumes the latency was already good to begin with. If we are already in the three-digit millisecond zone, which is very common at sub-60 frame rates, it won't matter how little of an impact frame generation adds. The latency will be very objectionable either way. 
For all of its flaws, upscaling is an actual solution to bad performance. Frame generation, however, is not.

text:
frame gen for me will always be terrible until flatscreen gaming can catch up to VR, VR games don't read inputs on a frame by frame level, they have the openXR API that reads inputs at a refresh rate equal to the refresh of the tracking technology, whether that be base station (index) or inside out (quest). This all means that when VR does frame insertion, the generated frames can read inputs just like real frames and update accordingly, leading to lower latency with frame insertion not higher, technically when measured by overall PC latency it is higher, but the in headset click to photon latency is lower, this is since the inputs are not tied to framerate (which is why if a VR game is running really badly you can move your head and literally see the desync between the frame and input, you can see the frame move slower then your head)

Until flat gaming can catch up, frame generation will be terrible, as long as inputs are tied to framerate its going to suck

Edit: I also know that LTT has a video showing off a tech demo that was made proving this is indeed possible, after all a mouse can have a pulling rate of up to like 10 thousand meaning if your game is running at 100 fps you have 9900 inputs the game is not reading, even ignoring frame gen, inputs shouldn't be tied to frame rate anymore as devices are updating significantly faster then games are running, and the way it could be done is the same way VR does it, a driver level API that feeds the absolute most recent input, not the input that was received when the frame started rendering

text: @ThrasherEscapes  I remember when LCD monitors started to become the norm and after all analog CRT's, which had input lag of 0ms, LCD's felt slow and sluggish. LCD with 30ms lag was considered barely acceptable but many were even worse. Now technology eventually caught on and LCD (and oleds) finally have low enough input lag that it doesn't matter anymore even for competitive gaming, especially now that refresh rates are high enough. Lo and behold, we are back in the lag city with frame generation. At least two frames of buffering lag if I have any understanding on how this technology works, starting frame and ending frame where the GPU can inject the generated frames in between. Not horrible if your raw FPS is high enough that the lag is beyond what a human can feel (however it is still detrimental for competitive gaming). But if you are at 40fps the frames are starting to be so slow that you can feel if they get delayed by two frames, maybe even more. We shall see what kind of tricks Nvidia manages to pull off but AFAIK it is not magic. Motion interpolation is old technology and while GPU's can do it better, faster and be more advanced just because they have more data to work with rather than just the real frames itself (which is what, for example, TV motion interpolation has to do), it is still basically that. Analyze two real frames and inject fake frames between those with a best guess what they should look like, output them all and then move on to the next two frames. Or however many frames it needs to buffer for analyzing, two is just the best case scenario for lowest lag.

People have been saying that Moore's Law is dead for a while, and we are now seeing what that looks like in the consumer market. We will not see the same growth rate in raw gpu performance as we saw over the previous 30 years (look at current comparisons of TSMC wafer costs!), and these types of ai solutions will have to do more and more of the heavy lifting.

If you say "I hate FG and will never use it": fair enough, but note that the limits of physics are now working against the development of the type of gpu which you are advocating for. Maybe in future a 1200w, huge $5000usd GPU will finally be able to push 120fps in path traced games. But such a product is not feasible for the general consumer.

text:
After thinking about it a while, DLSS 4 seems really quite niche.
15 base FPS => 30 with DLSS 3 => 60 with DLSS 4 for example seems hardly worth it. At such low frame rates, inconsistencies in frame rate and input timing are a major issue. Gaining 30 visual FPS won't help much with the overall experience in these conditions.
60 base FPS => 120 with DLSS 3 => 240 with DLSS4 seems overkill in most cases. It may look a little bit better on high refresh rate displays, if the artifacts are under control, but that's also not really a major benefit.

So the range in which x4 frame gen makes for a genuine notable improvement over x2 seems quite limited to me. Although it does excite me for Cyberpunk with path tracing at 4K in particular, since that falls right into the FPS sweet spot of about 30-50 base FPS.

And the whole "5070 = 5090 performance" I'm calling BS on now. Anyone buying the 5070 thinking that is gonna be disappointed. I'm 99.99% confident the useful lifetime of the 5070 will be severely impacted by Nvidia cheaping out on the VRAM and only giving it 12GB. And this junk about it being enough because it's GDDR7 is hilarious. Just for comparison not only dose the 4090 have 24GB of VRAM. But it's memory bandwidth is a little over 1 TB/s compared to the 5070 at 672 GB /s. Heck my RTX 3080 feels like it's just starting to show it's age. Most of all due to the 10GB of VRAM. Indiana Jones for example, I get a VERY solid 60 FPS with everything on at least high. But if I turn the texture cache up above high I run out of VRAM causing the game to plunge to ~5-7 FPS. 99% sure it's not a memory leak because I've had ~5+ hour play sessions with zero issue, it's only if I try to increase to many settings that impact VRAM usage. Path tracing in the game isn't even available to turn on without at least 12 GB VRAM. FF7 Rebirth has a note in its min requirements saying  you need at least 12GB of VRAM to play at 4K 30 FPS, low settings. That 12 GB frame buffer is 100% going to hurt the useful lifetime of the 5070. It's why the 5070Ti is the lowest model I'm considering. But thinking I may wait a bit, the performance gap between the 5090 and 5080 is gigantic. Of course there is going to be a 5080 Ti/Super etc. There is room between those two models for plenty of SKU's.

text:
@goncaloaraujo6644  Frame Generation can never decrease latency. The minimum latency is directly tied to the minimum FPS generated under normal conditions by your PC (which itself is the total latency affected by all parts of your mainboard communications, then CPU and GPU work speed to create the frame itself). So for example; assuming your system can consistently output 60FPS, this is then equal to a minimum play frame time of "16ms".

Any generated additional frames will have to wait for 16ms for a real frame to be generated, THEN the additional ms cost to compute. So after that initial 16ms, generate that frame, THEN it add to the pipeline IN QUEUE to be sent to the VDU for you to see it.
author: @fredsas12

text:
@goncaloaraujo6644  Yeesh, you're right, it is obvious - but it's you. Frame Gen literally cannot get you better latency results, because those extra frames do not respond to input, with the only possible exception (which we don't even know for sure yet) being camera movement now with Frame Warp. ONLY the native frames respond to all input, and therefore only the native FPS can have the best latency ("native" meaning using DLSS without FG). It's a hard cap on the performance of Frame Gen.

Any improvement of DLSS+FG over no DLSS at all is due to non-FG features making up the difference. It could be better than stock, but it will always be better for latency to just disable frame gen and leave the rest of the DLSS suite enabled.

text:
@GalaxyXYZ888  "Reflex" can only tighten up the latency for a system, not magically give it less. If your system already had higher average latency due to its components, e.g.; higher latency RAM timings, Spectrum "noise" on the mainboard, voltage droop etc, etc, then it will not do very much. Nvidia reflex and AMD anti-lag would be useless in these scenarios. Most systems however do not operate at max performance mode, they are usually in some sort of hardware balanced power configuration.

In-fact, simply putting the Windows power plan into "performance" mode, or even better, "Ultimate Performance" will act to minimise latency times across all hardware and thus the operating system. One cannot get less latency by activating these gimmicks, especially if they are running a capped below GPU performance threshold, i.e.: a V-sync off with FPS cap, as the system is already giving the lowest latency possible.

text:
How are you testing the input lag exactly?
If you're playing at 120FPS, then you have to add 8.3ms to 2x frame gen, and 25ms to the 4x frame gen. You can't count the intermediate frames as the reference frame of input, because they're transitionary.
Basically input lag is 51ms for no framegen, 66ms for 2x frame gen, and 82ms for 4x framegen (hypothetically, since I'm assuming 120FPS, which is likely not the case)
This is because frame lag from shooting a gun or interacting with a button feels VERY different from frame lag from controlling the camera. Which is why consoles get away with pre-historic framerates, but the moment you start using a mouse, anything below 60FPS feels bad.

bro...Nvidia cant fix this really. Its an issue from the game devs. Nvidias driver will happily produce the proper shader pipeline for you, you just have to ask the driver BEFORE you need the asset.
When using Vulkan or DX12 the devs themselves need to prepare the pipeline in advance, Pipeline stutter is almost exclusively a UE5 issue because even on UE3 the engine loads shaders at draw time per default, this wasnt an issue with DX11 and previous because it worked differently.
Stutter in UE is an Epic Games issue, not Nvidia..I mean you will have stutters when you run AMD / Intel cards too, so idk why you said this....

Raw performance numbers are far less impressive. The 5090 is about 30% faster than a 4090 but the 5080 and 5070 seem to be less than 10% faster over the baseline (non-Super) 40-series 4080 and 4070.

text:
As someone that has been playing Cyberpunk extensively recently, it completely depends on the scenario and your own perception. You will see way more blurriness and artifacting on Youtube videos because Youtube's bitrate and compression are very subpar by modern standards. If you're playing in person, it still varies wildly. If you're near Jig-Jig Street, it'll look substantially worse (whether just using base DLSS or frame gen) because you have both a lower base raster frame rate but you also have a resolution drop via base upscaling to compensate for the lower frame rate. But if you're in an area where performance is more stable, it'll look absolutely fine in most cases. I can't speak for multiframe gen, but odds are it's going to be pretty much the same as far as clarity goes.

As for "Nvidia told you not to do so," it is literally explained that he was given a mere five hours to work with. I know everyone in the Youtube comments thinks they can do everything better than everyone else, but that is not nearly enough time to work with every small facet and detail of this new tech, especially when trying to compare FPS numbers to both different options of the new tech but also against older tech. DF doesn't just use the in-game benchmark tool because it isn't reliable with conveying realistic performance numbers, so they have to go out and capture all this footage for themselves and hope that nothing insane happens that could break their sequence (like a car randomly spawning in the ground and exploding and/or spawning millions of particle effects from the crash collision).

This is a very surface-level review at its core, but the tech literally isn't even ready for release yet and there is still about a month before any of this is even close to being finalized. We'll probably see a much more in-depth review a few days before launch, or maybe a few days after because DF spends a lot of time and effort into their editing techniques.

​ @ronijs19 That is not true. If you have 60 fps without FG, then you only get latency equivalent to 30 fps with FG on, as you have to wait for an extra frame before FG can interpolate what's in-between.

Hence you need 120 fps to start without FG in order to get a latency equivalent to 60 fps with FG on.
But here is the issue (at least with current 40-series cards) there is a large performance penalty at using FG at 120 fps base framerate, so your base performance tanks to ca 80 fps, = 160 fps after FG. But 80 fps/2 = latency of 40 fps, which feels sluggish.

text: It'll become standard because we are hitting a hard limit of transistor size. We're already down to 3-4 nanometers per transistor across CPUs and GPUs, once you hit 1nm you start running the risk of dealing with performance loss due to quantum tunneling (yes, that is a real thing). You can always just make bigger chips in general, but they will output more heat and use way more electricity and cost way more too, AMD used to do this with two GPU chips on a single card. So AI-enhanced performance is going to become a commonplace thing in any game that strives for high graphical fidelity. Luckily for those that dislike that concept or notion, indie games still exist and can utilize retro art styles to capitalize on performance without looking bad if executed correctly.

text:
@saphyre-l4w  It's not counterintuitive at all. Frame gen increases latency, which is clearly shown even in your example. It obviously isn't free. Reflex just decreases it more than frame gen is increasing it, which isn't surprising either. Since Reflex is completely independent from frame gen I don't even see why you're bringing it up. The big discrepancy in input latency doesn't come when you compare 60 fps native to 240 interpolated, but when you compare 240 native vs. 240 interpolated. If you 4x your frame rate natively, your input lag decreases roughly by 4x. If you achieve it through interpolation, your input latency increases slightly. 

In other words, it's not the cost of frame gen that's the problem, it's that it doesn't serve as an alternative path to better performing games. Frame rate and performance is only synonymous when every frame is a ground truth update (calculated frame), not an interpolated frame. Frame gen is just motion smoothing, which has value for high refresh monitors, but it has nothing to do with performance.

text:
@ArchieBunker11  Base performance of the 5070 is much lower than the 4090. For example, 4k 120fps with FG on a 4090 means roughly 4k 60fps base. The 5070 can also do 4k 120fps thanks to 4x FG but the base was 4k 30fps. Frame generation from a 30fps base is terrible and will be a far worse experience.

Double the 4090 latency, then add 5ms. 
30ms latency on 4090 = 65ms latency on 5070.


So the 4x frame gen on 5070 is only worth using if you can already hit a stable 60+ fps at those settings/resolution and are targeting 240hz. 4090 is nearly twice as powerful and will always be able to achieve a much higher base quality or starting frame rate.
author: @AlexConnor_

text:
@Foetoid2k6  Nope. Double the latency, then add 8ms. To match 4090 visual settings and resolution a 5070 will be starting from half the frame rate, IE 30fps vs 60fps. Then 4x 30fps to 120hz and 2x 60fps to 120hz. So latency will be twice as bad on the 5070, plus the extra 8ms from running 4x FG vs 2x FG.

Completely unplayable unless you turn down settings on the 5070 to hit a 60fps starting frame rate, just like current DLSS FG is absolutely terrible unless you already have a good base frame rate.
